sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Subsurface conditions may deviate significantly from exploration interpretations, and construction operations can alter in-place soils and adjacent stability. An experienced geotechnical engineer should observe construction to identify field concerns and recommend design adjustments. The geotechnical report should discuss anticipated conditions at the footing bearing level for inspection staff.
sections.body: (p. 137) Because of the limitations of geotechnical explorations and geologic interpretations, there is always the possibility that significant deviations from anticipated subsurface conditions might be encountered. In addition, construction operations can change the behavior of in-place soils, as well as the foundation support and stability of nearby facilities. Therefore, observations by an experienced geotechnical engineer during construction are recommended to identify additional concerns in the field and to provide adjustments to the design when necessary. The contracting agency's construction personnel normally provide inspection and monitoring. The geotechnical report should discuss anticipated ground conditions at the footing bearing level and the geotechnical engineer should explain to the inspection staff how to identify the expected ground conditions and make sure the inspectors know how to contact the designers if questionable conditions are observed. Geotechnical staff may need to make site visits to observe questionable subsurface conditions and to oversee specialized instrumentation. Further guidance on inspection and monitoring is in the Guide to Earthwork Construction (TRB, 1990).
key_points: Subsurface conditions may deviate significantly from geotechnical exploration interpretations
Construction operations can change in-place soil behavior and stability of nearby facilities
Experienced geotechnical engineer observation during construction is recommended
Geotechnical report should describe anticipated conditions at footing bearing level
Inspection staff should know how to identify expected ground conditions and contact designers
Geotechnical staff may need to make site visits for questionable conditions or specialized instrumentation
Further inspection and monitoring guidance: Guide to Earthwork Construction (TRB, 1990)
sections.applicability: General guidance on the need for geotechnical inspection and monitoring during shallow foundation construction.

sections.title: Inspection
sections.summary: Inspection is only as good as the inspector; a competent inspector follows systematic inspection and documentation, communicates with the designer and reviews the plans, specifications and geotechnical report. Accepting other materials or procedures, or exceeding criteria (over-compaction behind an abutment), can cause distress. Sump dewatering with sidewall seepage can destabilize excavation slopes; dewatering in clay can induce consolidation. Probe excavation bottoms with rods, or use CPT and nuclear densometers; avoid test pits into the bearing stratum.
sections.body: (pp. 137-138) Inspection of foundation construction is only as good as the qualifications and experience of the inspector. Most problems can be avoided by having, besides a qualified and cooperative contractor, a competent inspector who follows systematic inspection and documentation procedures and communicates issues with the foundation designer. The inspector should be aware of conditions that could affect the intended performance of the foundation and structure, by reviewing the plans and specifications with the geotechnical report and consulting the geotechnical engineer. Foundations are usually designed to perform within settlement tolerances, maintain an adequate safety margin against bearing capacity failure, provide frictional resistance against sliding, provide resistance against lateral earth pressures, and provide sufficient support to prevent slope instability. Accepting materials or procedures different from those specified could compromise the design intent and lead to distress or failure; exceeding a criterion can also cause problems, such as over-compaction behind an abutment wall increasing stresses on the foundation element. Ground water impacts can be serious, possibly disturbing in-place soils; where dewatering may be necessary it should be mentioned in the construction considerations section of the geotechnical report. Sumps and dewatering wells affect foundation soils and slopes differently: the stability of temporary sloped excavations may be compromised if water seeps directly from the sidewalls for removal from a sump, where wells would locally lower the ground water level and improve slope stability; conversely, dewatering in a clay soil profile can induce consolidation settlement through the increase in vertical effective stress, which the settlement computations may not have allowed for. Improper construction methods can lead to foundation and slope failures; the inspector should regularly (e.g., daily) observe foundation and slope conditions for weaknesses the geotechnical engineer may need to address. Surface water and precipitation can deteriorate bearing materials: if the bearing materials are moisture sensitive, the geotechnical report should say so and recommend protection from surface moisture; some rocks and IGMs can also be adversely affected by moisture, seepage and relaxation due to excavation. Footing excavation bottoms can be probed with small diameter rods to confirm bearing resistance; cone penetration tests and nuclear densometers give more quantitative information. Test pits into and below the bearing stratum should be avoided because the backfill is difficult to compact. Routine inspection checks that procedural requirements are followed, materials meet performance criteria and compaction/density test results are satisfactory, and the inspector should review the geotechnical report for special issues to observe.
key_points: Inspection is only as good as the inspector's qualifications and experience
The inspector reviews plans, specifications and the geotechnical report and consults the geotechnical engineer
Foundations are usually designed for settlement tolerance, bearing capacity margin, sliding, lateral earth pressure and slope stability
Accepting non-specified materials or procedures can compromise design intent; over-compaction behind an abutment wall increases stresses
Dewatering needs should be mentioned in the construction considerations section of the geotechnical report
Sump dewatering with sidewall seepage may compromise excavation slopes; wells lower the water table locally and improve stability
Dewatering in a clay profile can induce consolidation settlement the design may not have considered
Inspector should regularly (e.g., daily) observe foundation and slope conditions
Moisture-sensitive bearing materials: report should recommend protection; some rocks and IGMs degrade with moisture, seepage and relaxation
Probe excavation bottoms with small rods; CPT and nuclear densometers for quantitative data; avoid test pits into the bearing stratum
sections.applicability: Inspection procedures and critical observations during shallow foundation construction.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Materials inspection is treated under 10.2.1 Line, Grade and Bearing Elevation, 10.2.2 Bearing Stratum and 10.2.3 Structural Fill Materials; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 138) No text is printed under this heading; see 10.2.1 Line, Grade and Bearing Elevation, 10.2.2 Bearing Stratum and 10.2.3 Structural Fill Materials.
key_points: Materials inspection: line, grade and bearing elevation (10.2.1), bearing stratum (10.2.2), structural fill materials (10.2.3)
sections.applicability: Overview of material inspection requirements for shallow foundation construction.

sections.title: Line, Grade and Bearing Elevation
sections.summary: Confirm that surveyed footing locations and elevations conform to plans and shop drawings. Any deviations from specified elevations or locations should be documented and checked with the designer for concurrence.
sections.body: (p. 138) The agency inspector should confirm that surveyed locations and elevations of footing elements conform to the plans and shop drawings. Where foundation elevations and location vary from those specified, the actual dimensions should be documented and then checked with the designer for concurrence.
key_points: Confirm surveyed footing locations and elevations match plans and shop drawings
Document and check with designer any deviations from specified elevations or locations
sections.applicability: Verifying footing location and elevation during construction.

sections.title: Bearing Stratum
sections.summary: The in-place bearing stratum must be verified against conditions anticipated in the geotechnical report. Some soils can be remolded and weakened by construction disturbance. If conditions deviate from expectations, consult the geotechnical engineer to determine if additional preparation measures are required.
sections.body: (p. 138) The in-place bearing stratum of soil or rock should be checked to verify the in situ condition and the degree of improvement achieved by the contractor's preparation approach. Some soil types can become remolded and weakened from disturbance. If conditions deviate from those anticipated in the geotechnical report and/or plans, the geotechnical engineer should be consulted to determine if additional measures are necessary.
key_points: Verify in situ condition of bearing stratum and effectiveness of contractor's preparation
Some soils can be remolded and weakened by construction disturbance
Consult geotechnical engineer if conditions deviate from those anticipated in the geotechnical report
sections.applicability: Verifying bearing stratum conditions during shallow foundation construction.

sections.title: Structural Fill Materials
sections.summary: Structural fill requirements should be strictly adhered to because the fill must perform within expected limits for strength (bearing capacity) and, more importantly, within tolerance for differential settlement. Small fill areas such as abutment and wingwall backfill may need smaller compaction equipment.
sections.body: (p. 139) The fill requirements should be strictly adhered to because the fill must perform within expected limits with respect to strength (bearing capacity) and, more importantly, within tolerance for differential settlement. Sometimes the area for construction of the fill is small, such as abutment and wingwall backfill, which may necessitate the use of smaller compaction equipment.
key_points: Fill requirements must be strictly followed for bearing capacity and differential settlement performance
Small construction areas (abutment/wingwall backfill) may require smaller compaction equipment
sections.applicability: Inspecting and verifying structural fill materials during shallow foundation construction.

sections.title: Monitoring
sections.summary: When monitoring structural fills under shallow foundations, test gradation and durability often enough, obtain the specified compaction and verify any surcharge unit weight. Check foundation elevations before and after structural load as a baseline for long-term bridge monitoring. Over soft soils it may be important to check that fill settlement is complete (settlement plates, horizontal inclinometers). Lateral movement can exceed vertical. Neighboring ground and facilities may need survey lines, telltales or instruments, and condition surveys.
sections.body: (p. 139) When monitoring the construction of structural fills that will support shallow foundations, particular attention should be paid to the following: the material should be tested for gradation and durability at sufficient frequency to ensure the material placed meets the specification; the specified level of compaction must be obtained in the fill, with testing, if applicable, performed by standard operating procedures and at the recommended intervals or number of tests; and if a surcharge fill is required for pre-loading, its unit weight should be verified to meet the value assumed in design. The elevation of constructed foundations should be checked before and after the structural load is applied, as a baseline for long-term bridge monitoring; later survey measurements can confirm satisfactory performance or identify potentially harmful settlements. It may be important to check the completion of fill settlements before foundation construction if soft compressible soils exist below (e.g., settlement plates, horizontal inclinometers). The lateral displacement potential can be greater than the vertical movements, so if conditions warrant monitoring may include complete survey coordinates and possibly more accurate instrumentation. Monitoring may also be needed to evaluate the impact on neighboring ground and facilities, with simple survey tag lines (benchmark and monitoring hubs) and telltales for lateral deviations and vertical subsidence/heave; higher reliability expectations may require inclinometers, strain gages, extensometers and tiltmeters. Pre-existing condition surveys of neighboring structures can be valuable, particularly in congested urban areas. The instrumentation program should be developed considering the anticipated performance, risks and potential consequences; parameters critical to project success should be identified and appropriate instrumentation selected. A key to successful use of instrumentation is to measure, plot and interpret the data in a timely manner so that corrective measures can be taken if needed.
key_points: Fill monitoring: gradation and durability tests at sufficient frequency; specified compaction obtained; surcharge unit weight verified against design
Check foundation elevations before and after structural load application for long-term monitoring baseline
Survey measurements confirm performance or identify potentially harmful settlements
Check that fill settlement is complete before foundation construction over soft compressible soils (settlement plates, horizontal inclinometers)
Lateral displacement potential can exceed vertical movements; complete survey coordinates if warranted
Neighboring ground: survey tag lines, benchmark and monitoring hubs, telltales; inclinometers, strain gages, extensometers, tiltmeters for higher reliability
Pre-existing condition surveys of neighboring structures are valuable in congested urban areas
Identify the parameters critical to project success and select instrumentation for anticipated performance, risks and consequences
Measure, plot and interpret the data in a timely manner to take corrective measures
sections.applicability: Monitoring construction and long-term performance of shallow foundations and structural fills.
